reason: The note on the VPC page states verbatim that every function runs in a VPC owned and managed by Lambda, not visible to customers, and that VPC configuration has no effect on it.

Under Shared responsibility model, 'these updates' are the security updates of the preceding sentence; Lambda applies them by default to managed runtimes, and container image users rebuild and redeploy.
Quote states every 10 seconds at most 1,000 additional execution environments or 10,000 additional requests per second per function; the bold sentence above gives the per-Region scope.
Quote says Lambda does not accrue unused portions of the scaling rate and the rate is always 1,000 concurrency units at maximum.

Quota table row: Concurrency scaling rate, default 1,000, Adjustable No, with the description of 1,000 additional concurrent executions every 10 seconds per synchronously invoked function up to the account limit.
The two quotes state cron and rate schedules, one-time invocations, flexible time windows, retry limits, maximum retention time, and asynchronous invocation of the function.
Quote matches the claim word for word: check response and retry; the CLI and SDK retry on client timeouts, throttling and service errors.
The note recommends Secrets Manager instead of environment variables for database credentials and sensitive information like API keys or authorization tokens.
The note states self-managed S3 code storage does not change the maximum .zip package size, which remains 250 MB unzipped.
Quote says Lambda references the code in your bucket, does not store a copy, and the code does not count against the Lambda-managed storage quota.
The opening paragraph of What is AWS Lambda states every part of the claim verbatim.
Quote: for a user Lambda considers identity-based and resource-based policies; when a service such as S3 calls the function, only the resource-based policy.

The claim drops a condition: the next line of the same SnapStart Pricing section says SnapStart pricing does not apply to supported Java managed runtimes; the quote supports the cache (3-hour minimum, then per ms) and restore charges only outside that exception.
Quotes state SnapStart works only on published versions and aliases to versions, not $LATEST, and Lambda initializes the function when you publish a version.
Quotes list Java 11+, Python 3.12+, .NET 8+ with base images across ZIP and container image formats, and say other managed runtimes such as nodejs and ruby and OS-only runtimes are not supported.
Quotes state the Firecracker MicroVM snapshot of memory and disk, encryption, caching, several copies for resiliency and automatic patching.
Quote matches the claim: no provisioned concurrency, EFS, S3 Files, or ephemeral storage greater than 512 MB.

Under When to use SnapStart, 'this latency' is one-time initialization latency; quotes give several seconds to as low as sub-second, best at scale, and provisioned concurrency in double-digit ms for strict cold start needs.
The claim and values are supported (table row and up to 66%), but the qualifier condition that Lambda Managed Instances bill EC2 instances covered by EC2 pricing options is not in any quote.
Batch size text: standard up to 10,000, FIFO maximum 10, and a batch size over 10 requires MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds of at least 1 second.
Parameter table row BatchSize: default 10, standard maximum 10,000, FIFO maximum 10.
Quote: with a batch window and very low traffic Lambda might wait up to 20 seconds, even when the window is set lower than 20 seconds.
Parameter table row MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds: default 0, batching window not supported for FIFO queues.
The function-code bullet of the backoff strategy states each part: stop processing and retrying, gradual backoff of ESM concurrency, message reappears after the visibility timeout.

The quote supports the 10-message default and the 5-minute batch window; the third part (invoke when the window expires, the payload quota or the batch size is reached) is only in the next sentence of the context, not in the quote.
Quote: SQS can send a repeatedly failed message to a DLQ, and AWS recommends maxReceiveCount of at least 5 to give Lambda a few retries.
Quote: by default up to 1,250 concurrent function instances per SQS ESM; provisioned mode scales up to 100,000 concurrent invocations.

The quote is one example in a list of configuration problems (role does not allow reading through the three actions); the 'must allow' requirement and 'local tests do not catch' are inferred from the surrounding context, not stated in the quote.

The quote is only the six-groups example; the general rule (FIFO queues, capped by message group IDs or maximum concurrency, whichever is lower) is in the preceding sentence of the context, not in the quote.
Quote matches the claim verbatim.
The note states the maximum concurrency setting and provisioned mode cannot be used at the same time.
The quote supports the 2 to 1,000 range; 'leaving it empty turns it off' is in the next sentence of the context, not in the quote.

The quote supports keeping reserved concurrency at least the total maximum concurrency or risk throttling; 'independent' settings and the per-event-source scope are only in the context, not in the quote.
Quote names partial batch response, ReportBatchItemFailures in FunctionResponseTypes, and making only the failed messages visible again.
Quote: provisioned mode scales 3x faster (up to 1,000 concurrent invokes per minute) and 80x higher concurrency (up to 100,000) than the default ESM.
Quote: each poller up to 1 MB/sec, 10 concurrent invokes, or 10 SQS polling API calls per second; Lambda adds up to 1,000 concurrency per minute between min and max pollers.
Quote gives MinimumPollers 2 to 200 (default 2), MaximumPollers 2 to 10,000 (default 200), and MaximumPollers at least MinimumPollers.

The quote is a recommendation (set a minimum of five when reserved concurrency is configured), but the fact is typed kind default with default_or_max default; the quote does not say five is a default.
Quote: function and queue must be in the same Region, although they can be in different accounts.
Quote: at low traffic Lambda scales back to five concurrent invokes and can optimize to as few as 2, not available with maximum concurrency; context gives the standard-queue scope.
